analysis.one_liner: Ends federal price supports and the quota system for peanuts.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: with zero cosponsors, it died in a House Agriculture subcommittee at the end of the 106th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law propped up the price of peanuts with government price support loans and restricted who could sell peanuts through a quota licensing system. This bill would have repealed both programs, ending price support for the 2000 crop onward and prohibiting any future federal price support for peanuts [S2] [S3]. It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it stayed until Congress ended [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy peanut products and taxpayers who fund the support program. The quota system limited legal peanut sales to license holders, keeping domestic peanut prices above world levels, and price support loans were backed by the government; repealing both would have lowered prices for buyers and ended a subsidy [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the peanut price support program and the peanut marketing quota system, which together raised peanut prices and channeled the benefit to a small group of license holders [S2] [S3].
Prohibits the Secretary of Agriculture from providing any future price support to peanut producers, while requiring settlement of loans already made [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Peanut quota holders, whose government-issued licenses to sell peanuts would lose their protected value, and peanut growers who relied on the price support floor [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: Ending the price support floor would have exposed peanut growers to lower and more volatile market prices, threatening farm incomes in peanut-producing regions [S2] [S3].
Quota holders had built their operations around licenses whose value depended on the quota system; abrupt termination, with no compensation, would have wiped out that value overnight [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have shifted money from a small set of quota holders and supported growers to consumers and taxpayers. The honest cost is that growers and quota holders faced real losses, and the bill offered no transition assistance; a phase-out with compensation, like the one Congress later adopted when it ended the quota program, would have been gentler on producers while still ending the consumer subsidy in reverse.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then a subcommittee, and no one ever scheduled it for a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Wu introduced the bill on July 22, 1999, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Agriculture [S1] [S5].
A week later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Risk Management, Research and Specialty Crops, where it remained with no further action [S5].
It expired at the end of the 106th Congress without ever receiving a vote in committee or on the floor [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Peanut quota holders and growers kept their price supports and quota-protected licenses, and consumers and taxpayers continued to pay for them. Congress went on to end the quota system three years later in the 2002 farm bill, with payments compensating quota holders for their lost licenses.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Peanut quota holders and supported growers

for.name: Rep. David Wu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to terminate peanut price supports and marketing quotas; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, referred it to a subcommittee, and never scheduled it for a markup or a vote.

against.name: House peanut quota holders and supported growers
against.role: Beneficiaries of the price support and marketing quota programs
against.what_they_did: Program beneficiaries whose licenses and price floors the bill would have ended; no member of Congress from a peanut state supported repeal, and the bill drew zero cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with no cosponsors, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.note: The quota system issued a limited number of licenses to sell peanuts for domestic use, and those licenses carried guaranteed high prices. Repealing the quota program would have eliminated the licenses' protected value, which is why the program survived until Congress ended it with compensation in 2002.

Growers gained from the price support floor and lost market access if they lacked a quota; ending the programs would have removed their guaranteed price floor but opened peanut farming to all producers and lowered consumer prices.
